text: A scheduled rule's query returns ordinary columns like UserPrincipalName or IPAddress, and to Sentinel those are just text and numbers unless told otherwise. Entity mapping, configured on the rule's Set rule logic tab, is what tells Sentinel which column represents a real entity — an Account, a Host, an IP address, a URL, a file hash — so it can be tracked as an object instead of a plain, disconnected string.

Each mapped entity has an entity type and an identifier describing what that column represents for it: an Account's identifier might be FullName, mapped from UserPrincipalName; an IP entity's identifier is Address, mapped from an IPAddress column. Sentinel supports entity types beyond these two as well, including Host, URL, FileHash, and Mailbox. Once mapped, every alert the rule generates carries real Account and IP entities, not just two columns that happen to look like a username and an address.

This mapping is the actual mechanism behind two things covered later in this path: the investigation graph, which visually maps how an incident's entities connect to other activity, and Sentinel's ability to correlate or link incidents that share the same entity. Neither works unless two rules mapped the same column to the same entity type in the first place.

An analytics rule with no entity mapping still generates alerts, but each one is just raw query output rendered as a flat table of columns. There's no entity page to open and no investigation graph to expand, so an analyst is left reading raw fields and manually hunting for related activity across other alerts instead of pivoting to it directly with one click.

Entity mapping is what turns two unrelated-looking alerts into visibly the same account showing up twice — the entire point of correlating detections into one coherent incident. Next, Lesson 12 puts the query, the schedule, and this mapping together into one real, working KQL detection rule.
